units.translation: for whom it is not fated to die.
with others I shall suffer what is fated.
for you will not escape fate any more.
it shrieked forth fated things from birds of the road to the royal house.
being within the fated nets,
for fate awaits both the free man.
fate has long been waiting.

for the marriage bed is fated for man and woman, where the reading μόρσιμοι in M has been rightly changed to μόρσιμος in the copies, wrongly to μορσίμη by Turnebus. For there was no necessity for the feminine ending in this place, nor is it read anywhere else: on which L. Dindorf spoke in Thes. vol. 5 p. 1204.
the fated lifetime was being fulfilled.

I would wish to meet with a fated noose, where since a noose is ineptly called fated and the meter, as the strophic verse shows, requires two short syllables, I, having removed the gloss βρόχου, conjectured προπρό, with μορσίμου used substantively without the article: on which see the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXIV.
whatever is fated for you, may it happen.
for you it is fated to be married, and for me to marry.

you will see neither the voice nor the form of mortals.
your tongue utters things similar in form.
one form of many names.
like to the forms of dreams.
destruction of form.
form and mind were distorted.
every manner of form leads the way.
nature is not of the same fashion as the form.
they have the forms of nocturnal apparitions.
for he will show two forms, where it is more probable that μορφά is in the dual number, as I said under δύο.

having died once for each shape.
resembling the shapes of dreams.
resembling mortal shapes.

the one-eyed Arimaspian host, on which see under μονόμματος.
Muse; song, music
which properly signifies the goddess of song, the tragedians also used it of song itself, especially Euripides, rarely Sophocles and Aeschylus, of whom there are two examples,
and let the singers sing a song of good omen at the altars.
it has seemed good to display a hateful song.
